item.title: Oil recap: crude slides as Trump holds off Iran strikes, OPEC+ hike stuck at chokepoints
item.description:
The scale of Monday's selloff suggests traders read the postponed strikes as a genuine de-escalation signal, even though Iran's denials of any active talks injected some doubt into that view. What stands out, though, is that the OPEC+ output increase did little to change the market's underlying supply calculus. With shipping through both the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait constrained, additional quota barrels are not straightforwardly reaching buyers, meaning the headline production increase is arguably a weaker bearish offset than the price reaction implies. Tanker rerouting around southern Africa and thinning Hormuz traffic point to a market where physical flow risk, rather than paper supply additions, remains the more important constraint. That disconnect between quota barrels and deliverable barrels is likely to stay in focus as long as both chokepoints remain under threat.

---

Crude tumbled on Trump's Iran reprieve, but with Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb both constrained, OPEC+'s latest output hike still can't easily get to market.

Summary:

  • Oil sold off from the Sunday evening Globex open through Monday's US settlement after Trump held off on strikes against Iran, at Iran's request and that of other Middle Eastern countries, contingent on a rapid deal.
  • Iran denied any direct talks with the US were under way and said it had no plans to host a US delegation or send its own representatives abroad in the near term, adding that separate talks with Oman on the Strait of Hormuz were unrelated to the US.
  • Trump said ahead of settlement that the Strait could be fully reopened within a day, with a second phase of talks to focus on Iranian denuclearisation, though the market's reaction to the comments was brief.
  • WTI traded roughly between the high $70s and low $80s per barrel over the session, while Brent traded roughly between the low $80s and mid $80s.
  • OPEC+ approved a September quota increase of close to 190,000 barrels a day, but the increase continues a pattern in which successive monthly hikes have failed to translate into meaningfully more oil reaching the market, given disruptions tied to the Iran and Ukraine conflicts.
  • Shipping data underscored those constraints: Bab al-Mandeb transits eased from Saturday to Sunday, Bloomberg estimated around 5 million barrels a day moving through Hormuz without transponder tracking, and Saudi tankers were seen rerouting around southern Africa.
  • Kuwait's July output rose to its highest since the Middle East conflict began, while Kazakhstan's output fell on export disruptions through the CPC.

Crude oil fell sharply over the session running from Sunday evening's Globex open through Monday's US settlement, as markets reacted to President Trump's decision to hold off on a fresh round of strikes against Iran. Prices gapped lower at the open and showed little inclination to recover through the day, even as Iranian officials pushed back on the idea that the reprieve reflected active diplomacy.

Trump had cancelled the planned attack over the weekend at the request of Iran and other Middle Eastern governments, on the condition that a deal could be reached quickly. Iranian officials, however, rejected suggestions that direct talks with Washington were under way. They said separate discussions with Oman concerning the Strait of Hormuz were not linked to any third party, and that outstanding issues with the US would be dealt with separately, later on. Iran added that it had no plans to receive a US delegation or send its own negotiators abroad in the coming days.

Later in the session, and ahead of settlement, Trump said discussions were focused on having the Strait of Hormuz fully reopened within a day, with a subsequent phase of talks to address Iran's denuclearisation. The market's response to those comments was brief and did little to alter the day's broader direction. By settlement, WTI had traded in a range of roughly the high $70s to low $80s per barrel, while Brent traded roughly between the low and mid $80s.

A key nuance running through the session was the limited practical impact of the weekend's OPEC+ decision. The group approved a September production quota increase of close to 190,000 barrels a day, but that addition continues a pattern seen through much of the year in which successive monthly quota hikes have not translated into a meaningful rise in oil actually reaching the market. The reason lies largely with the two chokepoints at the centre of current geopolitical risk. Shipping data from Kpler showed transits through the Bab al-Mandeb Strait easing from Saturday into Sunday, while Bloomberg estimated that around 5 million barrels a day were moving through the Strait of Hormuz without transponder signals, so-called dark flows. Six Saudi-flagged supertankers were seen rerouting around southern Africa in recent days in response to threats from Yemen's Houthi movement, even as two tankers carrying Saudi crude crossed the Bab el-Mandeb Strait over the weekend and traffic through Hormuz slowed following reports of vessel attacks. In effect, additional quota barrels approved by OPEC+ still have to navigate the same constrained routes as existing exports, meaning the headline supply increase carries less real-world weight than the number alone suggests. 

Elsewhere, production data added further texture. Kuwait's July crude output climbed to close to 2 million barrels a day, its highest level since the Middle East conflict began, while Kazakhstan's output slipped to around 1.85 million barrels a day amid disruptions to CPC export flows. Russia's seaborne crude exports from its western ports were expected to rise roughly 4 percent in August compared with July, according to trader estimates. A separate tanker carrying Russian naphtha also diverted around Africa in late July rather than risk the Bab el-Mandeb route, while Russia said it was stepping up protection for shipping in the Azov and Black Sea region and developing alternative export routes as attacks at sea between Russia and Ukraine escalated. Taken together, the session's price action reflected relief over the paused Iran strikes, but the underlying supply picture remains shaped less by OPEC+ policy than by whether oil can physically clear the world's most contested shipping lanes.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.
